q: An ionic bond is most likely to form between atoms of which pair of elements?
x: Potassium has a very low ionisation energy and fluorine a high electron affinity and electronegativity, so an electron is transferred to give K⁺ and F⁻. The other pairs are non-metals with small electronegativity differences and share electrons; carbon and chlorine is tempting because Cl is quite electronegative, but C–Cl is polar covalent.

q: In the carbon monoxide molecule, C and O are joined by a triple bond. How is this triple bond made up?
o: Three normal covalent bonds, each with one electron from C and one from O
One normal covalent bond and two coordinate covalent bonds donated by carbon
Two normal covalent bonds and one coordinate covalent bond donated by oxygen
Two normal covalent bonds and one ionic bond
x: Carbon has 4 and oxygen 6 valence electrons. Two pairs are shared normally (2 electrons from each atom), and oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to carbon as a coordinate bond, giving :C≡O: with an octet on both. Three normal bonds would need three electrons from oxygen and three from carbon and leave carbon short of an octet.

q: Metals such as copper and gold can be hammered into sheets and drawn into wires without breaking. In terms of metallic bonding, this is because:
o: The metal atoms are held by strong directional covalent bonds that bend easily
The metal ions and electrons form a rigid lattice of oppositely charged ions like NaCl
The valence electrons are fixed between pairs of neighbouring metal ions
Layers of positive metal ions can slide over one another while the delocalised electrons keep holding them together
x: In the electron-sea model the bonding is non-directional: when layers of ions slide, the delocalised electrons move with them and the attraction is kept, so the metal deforms instead of shattering. An ionic lattice shatters because sliding brings like charges together, which is the tempting but wrong comparison.

q: In the hydronium ion H₃O⁺, how many lone pairs remain on the oxygen atom, and how many of the three O–H bonds were formed as coordinate bonds?
o: One lone pair; one coordinate bond
Two lone pairs; one coordinate bond
One lone pair; no coordinate bond
No lone pair; two coordinate bonds
x: Water has two lone pairs on oxygen; one of them is donated to H⁺, giving one coordinate O–H bond and leaving one lone pair (once formed, all three O–H bonds are identical). Two lone pairs is the count for H₂O itself, the most tempting slip.

q: Which compound contains both ionic and covalent bonds in its solid, but no coordinate covalent bond?
x: NaOH is Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions (ionic), and the O–H bond inside the hydroxide ion is a normal covalent bond. NH₄Cl also has ionic and covalent bonds but its NH₄⁺ ion contains a coordinate bond, so it is excluded; KCl is ionic only and HCl is covalent only.

q: On moving down a group of the periodic table, the first ionisation energy generally decreases. The main reason is that:
o: The nuclear charge decreases down the group
The number of valence electrons decreases down the group
The atomic radius and the shielding by inner electrons increase, so the outer electron is held less firmly
The outer electron moves into a lower energy level
x: Down a group each element has one more shell, so the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded; this outweighs the larger nuclear charge. The nuclear charge actually increases, and the number of valence electrons stays the same within a group.

q: Which element has the highest second ionisation energy?
x: The second electron of sodium must come from the 2p subshell of Na⁺, which has the stable neon configuration close to the nucleus, so it needs far more energy (about 4560 kJ mol⁻¹). For Mg, Al and Si the second electron still comes from the third shell. Choosing Si follows the rule 'IE increases across a period' without noticing the change of shell.

q: The first four ionisation energies of element X are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10541 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group of the periodic table is X?
x: The big jump comes between the second and third ionisation energies, so X has two electrons in its outer shell and the third must come from an inner shell: X is in group 2 (the values are those of Mg). Group 1 is the slip of placing the jump after the first value.

q: The first ionisation energy of aluminium (578 kJ mol⁻¹) is lower than that of magnesium (738 kJ mol⁻¹), although aluminium has the larger nuclear charge. The reason is that:
o: Aluminium has a smaller atomic radius than magnesium
The electron removed from Al comes from a full 3s subshell
The electron removed from Al is a 3p electron, which is higher in energy and partly shielded by the 3s electrons
Aluminium has fewer electrons in its outer shell than magnesium
x: Mg loses a 3s electron, but Al (3s² 3p¹) loses its single 3p electron, which is higher in energy and shielded by the 3s pair, so it is easier to remove. Al does have the smaller radius, but that would raise, not lower, its ionisation energy.

q: For oxygen, O(g) + e⁻ → O⁻(g) has ΔH = −141 kJ mol⁻¹ and O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g) has ΔH = +780 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for O(g) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻(g), and why is the second step endothermic?
o: +639 kJ mol⁻¹; the second electron is added to a negative ion and is repelled by it
−921 kJ mol⁻¹; both steps release energy
+921 kJ mol⁻¹; the second electron enters a new shell
−639 kJ mol⁻¹; the second electron is attracted by the nucleus
x: Adding the steps: −141 + 780 = +639 kJ mol⁻¹. The second electron must be forced onto O⁻, which already carries a negative charge and repels it, so energy is absorbed. +921 comes from adding the magnitudes and ignoring the sign of the first step; O²⁻ has the neon configuration, so no new shell is entered.

q: According to VSEPR theory, what is the shape of the methanal molecule, HCHO, in which carbon forms a double bond to oxygen and single bonds to two hydrogen atoms?
x: Carbon has three electron regions (the C=O double bond counts as one) and no lone pair, so they point to the corners of a triangle: trigonal planar. Counting the double bond as two regions gives tetrahedral, the usual slip.

q: In SO₂, sulphur forms a double bond to each oxygen and carries one lone pair. According to VSEPR theory, the molecule is:
o: Bent (angular), with a bond angle a little less than 120°
Linear, with a bond angle of 180°, like CO₂
Bent, with a bond angle of about 104.5°, like H₂O
Trigonal planar, with three bond angles of 120°
x: Sulphur has three electron regions (two double bonds and one lone pair), arranged trigonally; the lone pair is not part of the shape, so the molecule is bent, and lone-pair repulsion closes the angle slightly below 120° (about 119°). Comparing with CO₂ ignores the lone pair; 104.5° belongs to four electron regions.

q: Which molecule is trigonal pyramidal in shape?
x: Phosphorus in PCl₃ has three bond pairs and one lone pair; the four pairs are arranged tetrahedrally and the three Cl atoms form a pyramid. BCl₃, SO₃ and NO₃⁻ have three electron regions and no lone pair on the central atom, so they are trigonal planar; BCl₃ is tempting because its formula looks like PCl₃.

q: According to VSEPR theory, how are the four electron pairs around the oxygen atom in a water molecule arranged, and what is the shape of the molecule?
x: Oxygen has two bond pairs and two lone pairs, which point roughly to the corners of a tetrahedron. The shape names only the positions of the atoms, so with two corners taken by lone pairs the molecule is bent. Calling the molecule tetrahedral confuses the arrangement of electron pairs with the shape.

q: A molecule XCl₃ has a trigonal pyramidal shape, and X forms only single bonds and keeps an octet. In which group of the periodic table is X?
x: A pyramidal AX₃ shape needs three bond pairs and one lone pair, i.e. 8 electrons around X. Three come from the Cl atoms, so X supplies 5 valence electrons and is in group 15 (as in NCl₃ or PCl₃). A group 13 atom gives a trigonal planar XCl₃ with no lone pair; a group 14 atom would be left with an unpaired electron.

q: What is the hybridisation of the carbon atom in carbon dioxide, CO₂?
x: Carbon forms two σ bonds (one to each O) and has no lone pair, so it needs two hybrid orbitals: sp, giving the linear shape; the remaining two p orbitals form the two π bonds. sp² is the slip of counting the double bonds' π parts as extra regions.

q: What is the hybridisation of boron in BF₃ and of nitrogen in NH₃?
x: Boron forms three σ bonds and has no lone pair: three hybrid orbitals, sp², planar. Nitrogen forms three σ bonds and also has a lone pair: four regions, sp³, pyramidal. Giving both sp² comes from counting only the bonds and forgetting nitrogen's lone pair.

q: Which type of hybrid orbital has 50% s character?
x: An sp orbital is formed from one s and one p orbital, so it is one half s. sp² has one third s (33%) and sp³ one quarter (25%). Choosing sp³ mixes up '50%' with 'four orbitals'.

q: How many σ bonds and how many π bonds are present in one molecule of benzene, C₆H₆?
x: Each carbon is sp² and forms σ bonds to two carbons and one hydrogen: 6 C–C σ plus 6 C–H σ = 12 σ. The six unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to give 3 π bonds (in the Kekulé picture of three C=C). Counting only the C–C σ bonds gives 6 σ.

q: In propadiene, CH₂=C=CH₂, what is the hybridisation of the central carbon atom, and how many σ and π bonds does the molecule have?
x: The central carbon forms two σ bonds (one to each CH₂ carbon) and no lone pair, so it is sp, with its two p orbitals making the two π bonds. Bonds: 2 C–C σ + 4 C–H σ = 6 σ, and one π in each C=C gives 2 π. Calling it sp² follows the 'double bond means sp²' habit without noticing it has two double bonds.

q: In molecular orbital theory, the bond order of a diatomic molecule is equal to:
o: The total number of electrons in bonding orbitals
The difference between the numbers of bonding and antibonding orbitals
Half the difference between the numbers of electrons in bonding and antibonding orbitals
Half the total number of valence electrons
x: Bond order = ½(bonding electrons − antibonding electrons); for H₂ it is ½(2 − 0) = 1. Forgetting the factor of one half doubles every bond order, the usual slip.

q: According to molecular orbital theory, what is the bond order of the C₂ molecule? (Consider only the 8 valence electrons.)
x: Eight valence electrons fill σ2s², σ*2s² and then four bonding electrons in the 2p bonding orbitals: bonding 6, antibonding 2, so bond order = ½(6 − 2) = 2. Three is the bond order of N₂, which has two more electrons.

q: Which of these molecules has a bond order of 2.5 according to molecular orbital theory?
x: NO has 11 valence electrons: 8 bonding and 3 antibonding (σ*2s² and one π*2p), so bond order = ½(8 − 3) = 2.5. N₂ and CO (10 valence electrons) have bond order 3, and O₂ (12) has 2.

q: Which diatomic species of period 2 has a bond order of zero according to molecular orbital theory?
x: Be₂ has 4 valence electrons in σ2s² and σ*2s², so bond order = ½(2 − 2) = 0 and the molecule is not stable. Li₂ (σ2s²) has bond order 1, B₂ has 1 and C₂ has 2. Li₂ is tempting because lithium is a metal, but in the gas Li₂ does exist.

q: According to molecular orbital theory, which of these species is paramagnetic?
x: N₂⁺ has 9 valence electrons, an odd number, so one electron must be unpaired: paramagnetic. N₂ (10) and F₂ (14) have all electrons paired, and O₂²⁻ (14 valence electrons) fills both π*2p orbitals completely, so these three are diamagnetic. O₂²⁻ is tempting by analogy with paramagnetic O₂.

q: The dipole moment of a polar bond is defined as:
o: The difference in electronegativity of the two bonded atoms
The product of the magnitude of the partial charge and the distance between the charges
The energy needed to break the bond into atoms
The ratio of the partial charge to the bond length
x: μ = q × r, so it has units of charge × length (C m, or debye). Electronegativity difference decides whether there is a dipole and roughly how big it is, but is not the dipole moment itself.

q: Which order of carbon–carbon bond length is correct?
x: More shared pairs pull the two nuclei closer: C–C about 154 pm, C=C about 134 pm and C≡C about 120 pm. Bond energy runs the other way (C≡C strongest), which is why the reversed order is tempting.

q: The enthalpy change for CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g) is +1664 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the average bond energy of a C–H bond?
x: Atomising one mole of CH₄ breaks four moles of C–H bonds, so the average is 1664 ÷ 4 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹. 1664 is the slip of forgetting there are four bonds; 333 comes from dividing by five atoms.

q: Bond energies: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242 and H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)?
x: Bonds broken: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ; bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ released. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ. +184 reverses the sign (formed minus broken), and +247 uses only one H–Cl bond.

q: Which molecule is polar even though its central atom has no lone pair?
x: In CH₂Cl₂ the carbon is tetrahedral with no lone pair, but two C–Cl and two C–H bond dipoles are unequal and do not cancel, so the molecule has a dipole moment. CCl₄, BF₃ and BeCl₂ are symmetrical with identical bonds, so their bond dipoles cancel. Thinking 'tetrahedral means non-polar' leads to rejecting CH₂Cl₂.
